concepts.name: Contiguous array storage and indexing
concepts.summary: Explain that an array stores elements contiguously so any element is reached by index in constant time, and that its size is fixed once allocated.

concepts.name: Linked list nodes and pointers
concepts.summary: Describe a singly linked list as nodes holding a value and a reference to the next node, reached only by following links from the head.

concepts.name: Stack last-in first-out
concepts.summary: Explain that a stack adds and removes only at one end, so the most recently pushed item is the first popped.

concepts.name: Queue first-in first-out
concepts.summary: Explain that a queue adds at the back and removes from the front, so items leave in arrival order.

concepts.name: Cost of insertion and lookup
concepts.summary: Recall in rough terms that array indexing is constant time while searching an unsorted sequence or inserting in the middle takes time proportional to the number of elements.

concepts.name: Key-value lookup with hash tables
concepts.summary: Recall that a hash table stores key-value pairs and finds a value by its key without scanning all entries.

misconceptions.text: A linked list lets you reach the nth element as fast as an array does.
A stack and a queue are the same structure because both hold items in order.
A hash table keeps its keys in sorted order.

concepts.name: Dynamic array resizing
concepts.summary: Implement an array that doubles its capacity when full and explain why appends are cheap on average.

concepts.name: Linked list insertion and deletion
concepts.summary: Insert and delete nodes in singly linked lists by rewiring references, handling head and empty-list cases.

concepts.name: Doubly linked lists and tail pointers
concepts.summary: Use previous links and a tail reference to make removal at a known node and appends at the end constant time.

concepts.name: Stack and queue implementations
concepts.summary: Build stacks and queues on arrays or linked lists, including a circular buffer, with constant-time operations.

concepts.name: Deque operations
concepts.summary: Use a deque to add and remove at both ends and recognise when it replaces a stack or queue.

concepts.name: Hashing and collision handling
concepts.summary: Apply a hash function to map keys to buckets and resolve collisions with chaining or probing.

concepts.name: Choosing a structure by operation costs
concepts.summary: Pick between array, linked list, stack, queue and hash table for a small task by comparing the costs of its main operations.

misconceptions.text: Appending to a dynamic array is always constant time in the worst case.
Deleting a node from a singly linked list is constant time given only the node's value.
A good hash function eliminates collisions entirely.

concepts.name: Hash table load factor and rehashing
concepts.summary: Analyse how load factor affects probe lengths and chain lengths, and why tables rehash into a larger array to keep operations near constant time.

concepts.name: Binary search tree operations
concepts.summary: Implement search, insertion and deletion in a binary search tree, including the cases for deleting nodes with zero, one or two children.

concepts.name: Tree traversal orders
concepts.summary: Perform in-order, pre-order, post-order and level-order traversals and state what each is useful for, such as in-order yielding sorted keys.

concepts.name: Binary heap and priority queue
concepts.summary: Implement a binary heap in an array with sift-up and sift-down to support insertion and extraction of the extreme element in logarithmic time.

concepts.name: Graph adjacency list and matrix
concepts.summary: Compare adjacency lists and matrices in memory use and in the cost of edge lookup and neighbour iteration for sparse and dense graphs.

concepts.name: Trie prefix storage
concepts.summary: Build a trie that stores strings by character along paths and use it for lookup and prefix queries in time proportional to key length.

concepts.name: Tree height and degeneration
concepts.summary: Analyse how insertion order determines binary search tree height and why sorted insertions degrade operations to linear time.

misconceptions.text: A binary search tree always gives logarithmic-time search.
A heap keeps all its elements in sorted order, so iterating its array gives sorted output.
An adjacency matrix is always the better graph representation because edge lookup is constant time.

concepts.name: AVL rotations and balance factors
concepts.summary: Analyse how balance factors detect imbalance after updates and how single and double rotations restore height balance while preserving order.

concepts.name: Red-black tree invariants
concepts.summary: Explain the colour and black-height invariants of red-black trees and how recolouring and rotations maintain them, bounding height at about twice the optimum.

concepts.name: Amortised analysis of structures
concepts.summary: Use amortised reasoning to justify costs of dynamic array growth and hash table rehashing, distinguishing them from worst-case and average-case bounds.

concepts.name: Collision strategy trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate linear probing, double hashing and chaining by clustering, deletion handling, memory overhead and cache locality.

concepts.name: Heap construction and heapsort
concepts.summary: Analyse why bottom-up heap construction takes linear time and how it supports in-place heapsort and top-k selection.

concepts.name: Memory layout and cache effects
concepts.summary: Evaluate how contiguity and pointer chasing affect real performance so that an array can beat a linked list despite equal asymptotic costs.

concepts.name: Balanced tree versus hash table choice
concepts.summary: Judge when ordered operations such as range queries and predecessor lookup justify balanced trees over hash tables, given worst-case guarantees and memory.

misconceptions.text: AVL and red-black trees are equally strictly balanced, so they perform identically.
Amortised constant time means every single operation is fast.
Two structures with the same Big-O costs will perform the same in practice.

concepts.name: Designing structures for workload
concepts.summary: Design or compose a structure from an access pattern, such as combining a hash table with a linked list to get constant-time least-recently-used eviction.

concepts.name: Evaluating adversarial and worst-case inputs
concepts.summary: Evaluate structures against adversarial input, including hash collision attacks, and choose randomised hashing or balanced trees to bound worst-case behaviour.

concepts.name: Cache-aware and external-memory trees
concepts.summary: Assess why wide-node trees such as B-trees minimise block transfers and when they beat binary trees in memory hierarchies.

concepts.name: Probabilistic and approximate structures
concepts.summary: Evaluate skip lists and Bloom filters by their expected costs, error rates and memory use against deterministic structures.

concepts.name: Concurrent and persistent structures
concepts.summary: Design or select structures that stay correct under concurrent access or keep older versions via structural sharing, weighing the overhead against simpler locking.

concepts.name: Graph representation for large-scale use
concepts.summary: Create a graph storage scheme such as compressed sparse rows that fits the graph's density, update rate and traversal pattern.

concepts.name: Proving invariants and bounds
concepts.summary: Evaluate and justify a structure's correctness and complexity bounds by stating invariants and using potential-function arguments.

misconceptions.text: Expected-case guarantees are enough in every deployment, so worst-case behaviour can be ignored.
Lock-free structures are always faster than lock-based ones.
Binary trees are optimal for any large dataset, so B-trees are only a database detail.
